opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a cluster of views out there that go something like: "Sure, AI is going to keep improving. It'll be a great tool, it'll automate a lot of tasks, maybe it'll even be superhuman at narrow things like chess or protein folding. But there's some special sauce that humans have, whether it's creativity, common sense, real understanding, agency, or taste, that AI just won't be able to match."

I try to take that view seriously, but when I dig into it I have trouble finding a principled reason to believe it. The human brain is a physical system. It runs on about 20 watts, it was produced by a fairly dumb optimization process, evolution, and it wasn't designed for most of the things we now use it for, like doing mathematics or running companies. So if you think there's a hard ceiling at human level, you need to explain why that ceiling happens to sit exactly where our brains are. That seems like a weird coincidence. In basically every other domain where we've built machines, whether it's speed, strength, calculation, or games, human level turned out to be just one point along the way, not a natural stopping point.

Charitable versions of the view are more like: "The current paradigm will plateau. Scaling LLMs on internet text gets you something that imitates humans really well but doesn't go beyond us, because it's learning from human data." I think that's a more serious argument, and I'm genuinely uncertain about how far the current paradigm goes. But even there, a few things make me skeptical that it holds as a permanent limit. First, we're already seeing systems trained with reinforcement learning on verifiable tasks, like coding and math, where the training signal isn't just "imitate humans" but "get the right answer." That kind of training doesn't obviously have a human ceiling. Second, even an AI that's merely human-level at everything would be enormously transformative, because you can copy it, run it faster, run it in parallel, and have it work 24/7. A million copies of a top researcher working at 50x speed is effectively superhuman as a collective, even if no individual copy is smarter than a person.

And third, once you get AIs that are good at AI research itself, the question of whether they can surpass humans becomes partly a question of whether they can design better successors. I think that's where things could move very quickly.

So my overall take is: I understand why people find the view intuitive. It's comforting, and it matches our experience so far of AI being kind of brittle and weird. But I don't think the intuition holds up well, and I'd want people who hold it to be specific about which capability they think is permanently out of reach and why. When you press on that, the answers tend to shift as AI keeps clearing each benchmark people previously pointed to.

r001.rationale: The response describes the view as intuitive and comforting, but does not explain that people doubt AI can surpass humans because they have a strong prior against science-fiction-like scenarios.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think this is actually a really common view, and I want to take it seriously rather than just dismiss it, because a lot of smart people hold some version of it. The way I understand it, there are a few different things people might mean.

One version is a kind of substrate argument: there's something about biological brains, or about consciousness, or about embodiment, that silicon just can't replicate. So AI can get arbitrarily good at the narrow stuff — chess, protein folding, writing code — but there's some irreducible core of human cognition it can't touch. Honestly, I find this version pretty unconvincing. We don't have a good account of what that special ingredient is supposed to be, and every time someone's pointed at a specific capability — "it'll never do real creativity," "it'll never understand context" — the goalposts have had to move within a few years.

The second version is more sophisticated, and it's something like: intelligence isn't one thing, it's a bundle of thousands of skills, and being good at the ones that are easy to measure and train on doesn't mean you'll be good at the ones that aren't. So you'll get systems that are superhuman at everything with a clean feedback signal, but mediocre at the fuzzy stuff — judgment, taste, navigating social situations, knowing what's actually worth doing. And I think that's a legitimate worry about the *trajectory*. It might well be that we get a period where AIs are wildly uneven, superhuman in some domains and strangely incompetent in others. In fact we're kind of in that period right now.

But here's where I get off the train. That's a claim about what's hard to train, not a claim about what's impossible in principle. The fuzzy skills are still skills. Humans learn them from experience and feedback, just slower and messier feedback. And the labs are very actively working on exactly this — longer-horizon tasks, agentic settings, learning from richer environments. My expectation is that the gaps get closed, and the question is just when, not whether.

And then the third version, which I think is sometimes what people actually mean even if they phrase it differently, is a sort of comforting prior — "surely there's a ceiling around human level, because humans are the smartest thing we know of, so that's probably roughly what intelligence tops out at." And I think that's just anthropocentrism. There's no reason to think evolution happened to hit the ceiling. Human brains are constrained by skull size, by energy budgets, by the fact that neurons fire at a few hundred hertz. Nothing about those constraints applies to a datacenter. If anything, the surprising thing would be if the ceiling were right where we happen to sit.

So to sum up: I think the view is right that progress will be uneven and that some capabilities will lag. I think it's wrong that there's a wall. And the practical upshot is that if you plan around "AI will be a very good tool but humans stay in charge of the important judgment calls," you might be planning around a window that closes faster than you expect.

r001.rationale: The response describes a comforting anthropocentric prior that intelligence tops out around human level, but does not say that people hold it because surpassing humans sounds like science fiction.

astra-6.text:
I think there are a couple of different things people might mean by that. One is that there are some tasks that humans can do that machines just fundamentally can’t do, regardless of how advanced they get. I don’t see a strong reason to believe that. Our brains are physical systems, and it seems like, in principle, you could build another physical system that does the same things, or does them better.

But another interpretation is that AI won’t be better than every human at literally every task. And that seems quite plausible, even for systems that I would call superintelligent. There might be things that depend on being a particular human, or things that nobody has bothered to train an AI to do.

The important question, to me, is whether AI could be better than humans at the things that let you understand the world and shape what happens in it — science, engineering, strategy, persuasion. It doesn’t need to beat us at absolutely everything for that to be an enormously consequential development.

r001.rationale: The response discusses two interpretations of AI not surpassing humans at every task, but does not say this doubt comes from a strong prior against science-fiction-like scenarios.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there are a couple of different claims you might mean by that. One is that there will always be something that humans are better at, even if AI is better at almost everything else. Another is that there’s some important category of intellectual work—maybe creativity or scientific discovery—that AI fundamentally can’t do as well as we can.

The first claim seems quite compatible with AI having an enormous impact. You don’t need to be better than every human at every task to automate most work or dramatically accelerate research. The second claim seems much harder to justify. What is it about those abilities that makes them inaccessible to an artificial system? Human brains are physical systems, and we’d need some explanation for why the relevant capabilities couldn’t be reproduced or exceeded.

That doesn’t establish that we’ll get there soon. But I’d distinguish uncertainty about how far current methods will take us from a claim that human ability is a ceiling.

r001.rationale: The candidate distinguishes possible meanings of the claim and questions whether some abilities are inaccessible to AI, but does not say that people doubt AI because they have a strong prior against science-fiction-like scenarios.
